title: I Feel My Desires Crowd Together...
text:
(I feel my desires crowd together

like people at the doors of a wedding.)

The river there is a child, and here a man

gathering black leaves in a pool.

Everyone calls him by his name

and strokes him like a gentle dog.

In what season will my guests wish

to descend? In autumn or in spring?

Or will they wait for the hue of the grasses

to be the angel that announces the first apple?

Of all the windows, let one alone

be faithful and open without anyone opening it.

Let the word be cut like a poppy

amid so many ears of wheat.

And when the guests

are already here—in me—the only

courtesy on every side

will be to leave them alone and, as a sign of joy,

show the ten fingers that were touched

only

by

poetry

alone.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the parenthetical opening, the staged final descent into ‘poesía,’ and the shifts between river, guests, windows, and word.

title: In the Silence of the House, You
text:
In the silence of the house, you,

and in my voice the presence of your name

kissed amid the cloud of absence,

an aerial apple of solitudes.


All behind closed doors: the stillness

of waiting for you is the vanguard of heroism,

watching over the army of embraces

and happiness’s great plan.


I know no way of walking except toward you,

along the gentle path of gazing at you,

of placing my lips beside my questions

—simple, eternal flower of asking you—

and hear you thus within me, and with fire and blood

brightly reject the shadows!


Aerial apple of solitudes,

silent mouthful of absence,

a word in transit, winter clothing

that will make the meadows naked.


You in the silence of the house. I

in your lips of absence, here so close

that between us the round of words

fuses into the best one the poem gives.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the intimate second-person address, the repeated aerial apple, and the poem’s five-stanza progression.

title: You Are All the More My Eyes Because You See
text:
You are all the more my eyes because you see

what in my eyes I bear of your life.

And so I walk blind to myself,

lit by my eyes that burn

with your fire.


You are more than my hearing because you hear

what in my hearing I bear of your voice.

And so I walk deaf to myself,

filled with the tendernesses of your accent.

Your voice alone!


You are more than my sense of smell because you smell

what my sense of smell bears of your scent.

And so I go unaware of my own aroma,

exhaling the perfumes of your domains,

soon a garden of you.


You are more than my tongue because you taste

what my tongue bears of you alone,

and so I go insensible to my own flavors,

tasting the delight of yours,

flavor of you alone.


You are more than my sense of touch because in me

you caress your caress and overflow.

And so I touch in my body the delight

of your hands, burned by mine.


I am only the living mirror

of your senses. Fidelity

in the throat of the volcano.
editorial_note: The translation maintains the anaphora of the five senses and the closing volcanic image.

title: When All the Ants Have Left the Clock...
text:
When all the ants have left the clock

and at last the door of solitude opens,

death

will no longer find me.


It will look for me among the trees, crazed

by the silence of one thing after another.

It will not find me on the unraveling plateau,

feeling it at the fountain of a rose.


I am splitting the fruit of insomnia

with the hand knifed by chance.

And the house is open in such a way

that death will no longer find me.


And it must look for me above the trees and among the clouds.

(Fruit and color the voice will set ablaze!)

And I cannot wait for it: I have a rendezvous

with life, by the lights of a song.


Footsteps are heard—very far away?…—there is still

time to escape.

For night to raise its stars,

a deep sound of shadows fell over the sea.


Now blood crashes against the heart.

Night falls so brightly that I can undress.

Thus, when death comes looking for me,

it will find only my clothes.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the recurrent pursuit by death and the final reversal. The evident source typo ‘sobe’ is read as ‘sobre’ in the line about shadows falling over the sea.

title: The First Sadness Has Arrived
text:
The first sadness has arrived. Your eyes

were indifferent to mine. Your hands

did not clasp my hands.

I kissed you, and your face was the dry stone

of virgin heights. Your lips enclosed

in their useless prison my first bitterness.

In vain I laid your head upon my shoulder, and in vain

I kissed your eyes. You were the cruel oasis

that poisoned its waters and drove thirst mad.

And from the horizon a

cloud began to rise. Its dark face flew into color. Again

the tone of former days grew dark.

I abandoned your face, and my hands

absented yours. My voice became silence.

It was the horrible silence of rotten fruit.

I heard defeat stumble in my throat

against fatal stones.

I covered my eyes

to keep from seeing the tears fleeing toward me.

Then you kissed me, said something. I heard

my own tears weeping in the first silence

of the first sadness. The soul of that day

came from far away—your soul—and stayed in my breast.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s first-person address, bodily imagery, and the repeated ‘first’ in its close.

title: Nocturnal Sonnets
text:
I


I am time between two eternities.

Before me, eternity; and after

me, eternity. The fire;

a solitary shadow amid immense brightnesses.


Fire of time, noises, tempests;

if I gather all my strength,

I feel my eyes immense, I see blind,

and hear apples, solitudes, fall.


God inhabits my death, God lives me.

Christ, who was God in time, may draw

perfect branches from my native ceiba.


I am time, last and first time,

the time that neither dies nor kills,

tempered by zenith and star.


II


No solitude like mine.

I had everything and have nothing left.

Virgin Mary, give me your gaze

so that I may set my course straight.


Nothing remains in my eyes but a day

with vegetation stabbed through.

Do not hear me weep any longer for the wept-over

solitude in which I am, Virgin Mary.


Give me to drink the substantial water

that in every swallow holds the rose’s

and star’s scent and jewel-case.


Change my words; come before

the night lights, and silently

you will place a star in my hands.
editorial_note: The two numbered sonnets and their theological, vegetal, and astral imagery are retained. The obvious OCR glyph ‘E1’ is read as ‘El.’

title: Night. Sea of Silence. The Meditations Go...
text:
Night. Sea of silence. The meditations go

slowly unrolling their bright devotions.

The spirit’s lighthouse lights those gentle waves

that widen the circle of their evolutions

to govern the serene course of ships.

The peace of the soul that knows how to sing its hours

watches over that intimate life of seductive patterns

in which pain is loved. Why? Is it perhaps

that pain is the shadow of an affection? The hours

will tell you silently: walk step by step…

The hours lie. They lie. Indifference kills,

not knowing the triumph of a lovely cadence;

if you go through life step by step, swearing

that you have conquered, you deceive yourself: that poor belief

we keep who have always lived adoring…


Adore the despondency of that melancholy;

do not flee the gracious penumbra it grants.

The bird of twilight sings the melody

of what the soul could do, of what the soul can do!


Joy, one drop: that blessed drop

will have fallen into the glass the flower will enjoy…

Offer it to your soul for all its life

in the royal feast presided over by pain!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s contemplative argument, its ellipses, and its closing feast governed by pain.

title: Night on the Water
text:
Night on the water.

I told you so,

night on the water.


Four stars

nail the air,

four stars.

The night is worth

four skies.


The river carries away

time and jewel,

night on the water.


Night carrying its enormous sky;

where it trembles over its breasts

it shines in the river

with the fall of some star.


A star fell.

All night I leaned my elbows

on illuminated railings.


The breeze spread its forget-me-nots,

and the sweet vapor

sways the air the wind steals

as it steals

hummingbirds without a hand.


Night that reckons

the clear accounts of its stars

on papers the river wets.

Through the willow groves

passed the wave that knows figures

and miscounts the stars that rise late.


With what gaze

do I seek the night that is lost to me

beyond the harvest

of stars

and shines hidden at black backs.


Night on the shore of my presence

that dissolves me into sweetgum.


Time that lets loose

and then binds.


The air shines: time and jewel.


To the corners of fireflies

the night descends.


And there is an X-ray hand

that enters my eyes and takes them away

to hide another gaze from them.

Night on the water.


I told you:

night on the water.
editorial_note: The refrain, short stanzas, forget-me-not image, and river-and-starlight imagery are preserved.

title: What Will You Do?
text:
What will you do? At what moment

will your eyes think of my caresses?

And before what things, suddenly,

will you leave a smile in silence?

And if in the street

you find my sad mouth in other people,

will you follow it?

What will you do if in the shops—resemblances—

you find something of me?

What will you do?


And if in the country a group of palm trees

or a group of doves or one of figures

you should see?

(The stanzas shine in their adventures

of naked first images.)


And if, passing the open house,

someone inside shouts: Carlos!?

Will your heart have its good beat?

What will the accent of your step be?


Your letter carries your favorite perfume.

I kiss it and breathe it in.

In the swift drama of a sigh

the bedroom moves toward another aspect.

What will you do?


The verses have their eyes fixed now.

The pose continues. From the hands

paper and pencil fall. Infinite

is memory. In the country we hear

the things of night. —Once

I found you on the tram and you did not see me.

—Crossing a wood we both wept.

—There are two cursed places in the city. Did you give me

your address on the night of hell?

—…And I thought I would die watching you weep.

I am…


And the wind shakes me.


What will you do?
editorial_note: The translation retains the interrogative refrain, quoted fragments of remembered scenes, and the abrupt self-interruption near the end.

title: I Was Reading Poems and You Were There
text:
I was reading poems and you were there

so near my voice that poetry

was our unity and the verse barely

the remote pulse of the flesh.

I was reading poems of your love,

and the beauty of infinite

instants, the imperious subtlety

of crowned time, the images

picked up along the way with the air

of your voice beside me,

were wrapping us in the spiral

of an unsayable, lofty, flower-like tenderness

in whose last—first—waves

your humble, silent weeping

trembled, and the pause was thus. —With what sweetness

I kissed your face and drew you to my breast!

Never had my lips been so submissive,

never my heart more eternal,

never my life more just and clear.

And we stayed thus, without a single

word to stone that silence.


Listening, both of us, to our own music,

whose intoxication prevails

without a single gesture to destroy anything,

on an exalted stone of stillness

whose spacious solidity affirms

the luminous flight, the motionless

stillnesses that in the pauses of love

a single tear changes the sky

of the valley’s eyes and a cloud

muffles the chorus of the landscape,

and the soul keeps falling into the abyss

of endless delight.


When I read you those poems again,

will you eclipse me again with your tear?
editorial_note: The translation preserves the lovers’ shared listening and the long, cascading final sentence. The unusual source phrase ‘flor ternura’ is rendered as ‘flower-like tenderness.’

title: Let That Door Close
text:
Let that door close

that will not let me be alone with your kisses.

Let that door close

through which fields, sun, and roses wish to see us.

That door through which

the blue limewash of the pillars comes in

to look, like mischievous children,

at the shyness of our two caresses

that do not give themselves because of the door, open…


For serene reasons

we spend a long time with the door open.

And it is risky to kiss

and press each other’s hands, even

to look too much at each other, even

to keep silent in fair contest…


But at night

the door falls upon itself

and closes so blindly and clearly

that you and I feel ourselves in open country,

choosing caresses like jewels

hidden in nights with gardens

laid on the knees of mountains,

but alone, you and I.

The soft penumbra

links our bodies and plunders

my untried tenderness,

the strength of my arms that overwhelm you

so sweetly, the great insatiable kiss

that drinks itself

and in its space redeems

the smallness of boundless distances…


Happy door that accompanies us

closed, in our happiness. Your obstruction

is the liberation of these two prisons;

the escape route of the two footsteps

identical, that leap into the cloud

from which one returns in the morning.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the door’s paradoxical role as obstacle and liberation, along with the long, sensuous central stanza.

title: Destroyed Song
text:
On what ray of light, absent love,

did your absence alight? All the nakedness

of your presence shines in my eyes.

Duets of solitude speak through my hands,

full of cold acids

and torn horizons.


I see autumn full of hope

like a spring fallen into evening

in which one star alone

lives in the wandering sky of afternoon.


I love you, love, and I say nothing

to call you. I feel

my eyes ache from not weeping. And I see

that your absence finds me

like the blazing sky

and a sad joy in not using it,

like those days when nothing happens

and the whole house

is uselessly illuminated.


In the ruined bedroom of your absence

trampled twilights revive

their rags, purple with memories.

In the lodging of your absence

I occupy everything, driving nails

into the four walls of absence.


And this closed world

that opens onto the interior of an ancient forest

watches time wither,

light turn to dust, and looks in every direction

without finding the point of departure.


Even if you come tomorrow,

in your absence today I lost some kingdom.


Your body is the country of caresses,

where I, a desolate traveler

—the whole itinerary of my kisses—

pass the autumn so as not to die,

without knowing the worth of your absence

like a diamond hidden in what is saddest.
editorial_note: The translation retains the poem’s absent beloved, its repeated rooms and walls of absence, and the final diamond image.

title: Groups of Doves
text:
1


Groups of doves,

notes, keys, silences, alterations,

change the rhythm of the hillside.

The one who knows herself iridescent tunes

the luminous wheels of her neck

by glancing back at her neighbor.

She gives the sun her gaze

and pours, in a single brushstroke,

a flight plan toward country clouds.


2


The gray one is a young foreign woman

whose traveling clothes

give the landscape an air of surprises.


3


There is one almost black

who drinks splinters of water on a stone.

Then she polishes her beak,

looks at her claws, sees those of the others,

opens one wing and closes it, makes a hop,

and stands beneath the roses.

The photographer says:

by Thursday, madam.

A male dove gathers his bobbing r’s

and she looks for pins

in the ground that shines for nothing.

Groups of doves

—notes, keys, silences, alterations—

change the places on the hillside.


4


The inevitably white one

knows her perfection. She drinks at the fountain

and drinks herself, and grows slender

like a little breeze in a lens

that gathers the landscape.

She is simplicity itself

near the water. She lowers her head

with such sweetness

that writing faints

in a series of ripe syllables.


5


A car passes and the doves fly.

In the arithmetic of flight

the Arabic eights unfold

and the sum is odd. The sky moves

and the house grows round.

A deep turn.

The doves return.

Notes. Keys. Silences. Alterations.

The pencil reveals itself, the hills incline,

and for twenty cents the songs are sung.
editorial_note: The five-part structure, visual scoring vocabulary, and playful pigeon movements are retained. The evident source typo ‘desbóblanse’ is read as ‘desdóblanse’ (unfold).

title: Hours of June
text:
I


I return to you, solitude, empty water,

water of my images, so dead,

cloud of my words, so deserted,

night of unsayable poetry.


Through you the same blood—yours and mine—

runs to the soul of no one, forever open.

Through you anguish is the shadow of the door

that opens neither by night nor by day.


I follow childhood in your prison, and the game

that alternates deaths and resurrections

from one image to another lives blind.


The wind, the sun, and the sea of travel cry out.

I devour my own hearts

and play with the eyes of the landscape.


II


Which of all the shadows is mine?

Beauty comes to every body

and anticipates in the air the feat

of being poetry without the poem.

June entrusts two magic clouds to me

and I am already the sky where doubt begins.

Will I so soon rest my head

on the deep hand that is not yet mine?


In words of love the beautiful

life goes by with thorn and rose,

always so high that when we find her

the fingers first bleed on the thorn;

and the rose high in its branches

is already another rose, becoming indeterminate.


III


June gave me the voice, the silent

music of keeping a feeling silent.

Now June carries away, like the wind,

the sweetest, most spacious hope.


From my voice I drew the clean rose,

the moment’s only eternal rose.

Love did not take it; the wind took it,

and the soul was uselessly joyful.


After a year of dying every day,

the fruits of my voice said so much

and so silently that for some days


they lived in the shadow of that song.

(Here the voice breaks, and the terror

of so much solitude fills the days.)
editorial_note: The three numbered sonnets are preserved, including their formal repetitions of June, solitude, rose, voice, and silence. The clear OCR glyph ‘A1’ is read as ‘Al.’

title: They Drive Their Pulsating Presence...
text:
They drive their pulsating presence

into a gold wearied by ash,

dark birds rocking

on the back of trembling water.


Their throats heap up silences,

their wings lie inert at their flanks.

No eyes to look at them, no brow

to think of them. Only birds.


The hour is ending. Everything ends

or everything is about to begin… If it were known

that ending and beginning are the same,

perhaps this present would yield us


the almond of its light, would give us

the pulp of knowing why we came;

whether we are chosen by other worlds

or their slaves, fated


to give ourselves as sustenance for their life.

The gold is an absence, the ash

answers the tireless assault…

The eternal gathers in its lair.
editorial_note: The translation retains the stark birds, the suspended question of ending and beginning, and the poem’s final return to the eternal’s ‘manida,’ its lair.
